text: The war had been over barely a year when František Čáp finished this account of sabotage inside an aircraft factory. Seventy-six minutes leaves no room for a chronicle, and Muži bez křídel does not attempt one: the occupier's reprisal machinery is already turning when the film opens, and what hangs on the work is not the outcome of a war but whether a shift of men can slow an assembly line and still be at their benches the next morning. It carries a Palme d'Or, which for a Czech-language film finished in 1946 means it travelled early. Pictures made this close to their material tend to be exact about method and cautious about heroism. Sabotage is arithmetic before it is courage: how much delay is worth how many names.

A lottery decides who leaves, and the prize is the last uncontaminated place on the planet. Everyone in Lincoln Six-Echo's world is fed, monitored and kept hopeful, and hope is the facility's instrument of order, issued in small amounts. That is the architecture of a chamber piece. The director is Michael Bay, so the chamber does not hold. What follows spends most of 136 minutes on pursuit at full studio expenditure, running on a premise that cheaper science fiction has usually handled in one room with two actors and a locked door. The film dates its own future to 2019, thirteen years ahead of the release and a period detail by now. A closed world stays closed only while nobody inside it has anything to compare it with.

The secret in this classroom belongs to the teacher, and one of his students is going to find it. Dan Dunne is good with junior-high kids and, away from them, an addict; when that comes apart, a child ends up holding an adult's private life and neither of them has anywhere to take it. Ryan Fleck keeps the film to 107 minutes and to the distance between two people, so the teaching is not uplift and the addiction is not a case study. What forms between them is tenuous by design, a bond neither can justify and neither can afford to end. The record around it runs mostly to actor's prizes, with a first-film citation from New York critics and the Independent Spirit for Fleck's direction. Small dramas earn that attention by finding the right register, and the register here is an ordinary school day with something intolerable inside it.

By the time these recruits arrive, the insurgency in Afghanistan is slowly winning. Fyodor Bondarchuk takes 139 minutes over the passage from training to posting, and the length is doing work: a unit is manufactured out of unrelated young men at roughly the scale on which it will later be spent. Nothing in the premise gives these men a view of the policy that placed them; they get the ground. The film was put forward as an international submission to the Academy Awards and took the Nika for best picture and for discovery of the year, the second of which suggests a country responding to something new in it rather than to its argument. Made in Russian in 2005, it arrives while the war is still inside living memory.

One schoolmaster's entire working life, from a nervous first term to the head's study, fitted into 114 minutes. Nothing here is built to surprise. The method is accumulation, and the wager is that a man seen often enough in the same rooms becomes someone an audience will sit with, which is a strange thing for a feature to attempt and a harder thing to sustain. Sam Wood directs it as a British school picture of 1939, in which manners carry what plot carries elsewhere, and the marriage at its centre is what converts a competent teacher into a fixture. It sits on the BFI's hundred British films, and the record around it runs heavily to acting and directing citations. The achievement being dramatised, in the end, is showing up.

A Finnish sniper, chained to a rock and left there, works himself loose in the days before Finland leaves the war. A Soviet captain under arrest by his own secret police gets away in the same stretch of September 1944. Both end up on one Lapland farm, where a woman named Anni takes them in and declines the categories the war has issued: ally, enemy, prisoner. Aleksandr Rogozhkin files the result as comedy as much as drama, which is accurate, since the war has left these three without a language in common and a farm is too small for a misunderstanding to stay private. The Silver George went to Rogozhkin for the direction, and the Russian state gave the film a prize of its own. A hundred minutes, three people, one house.

Cardiac surgery in communist Poland required two kinds of permission, and only one of them came from the body. Łukasz Palkowski takes 121 minutes over the early stretch of Zbigniew Religa's career, the part before anyone had agreed he was right, when a surgeon proposing to open a chest had to win the room before he could win the argument. The 1980s setting is not decor. What a hospital may attempt is set by what the state will supply, so a man working at the limit of his field is asking a system of fixed quantities for an exception, repeatedly, in writing. The Golden Lions at Gdynia and the Polish Film Award for best film both went to it. Biography usually arrives once the subject has been proved right; this one gets there earlier.

Jazz was the offence and clothing was the evidence, in a musical about young Muscovites in the 1950s. Valery Todorovsky's film took its Nika for costume design, which is exactly where its quarrel with the state is conducted: a Communist named Mels falls for a jazz fan named Polly, and his party membership turns negotiable the moment he is seen with her crew. Two hours and ten minutes is a long stretch for this material, and the musical form does what a straight drama could not, which is to make the disobedience enjoyable rather than brave. The numbers are how the film argues, and nobody in it has to make a speech. What a state loses first, in a story shaped like this, is not its authority but its claim on what a good time looks like.

A scooter business, a bank that wants collateral, and a man from the old building who has cash and asks for no paperwork. Krzysztof Krauze built this out of a real case, and the realism is procedural rather than atmospheric: 106 minutes on how a favour becomes a debt, a debt becomes a claim, and a claim becomes the whole of two men's waking attention. Poland in 1999 is a condition here rather than a backdrop, with private enterprise recently ordinary and the difference between a partner and a creditor still being improvised by everyone involved. Crime films tend to open on a decision to do something wrong. This one opens on two men who want a loan and are turned down by the institution that exists to give them one.

Comedy, drama, romance, and then thriller, for a story about a mother trying to marry off her daughter. Borys Lankosz runs the film between the present and Warsaw in the 1950s, and the older half is where the fourth genre comes from, since a suitor in that decade arrived with a political history attached to him. Sabina has just turned thirty and says little. Her mother says everything. Her grandmother, sharp-tongued and impossible to keep anything from, decides what the household is allowed to know. Ninety-nine minutes, three generations of women in the same rooms, and Poland put it forward to the Academy Awards. The centre of gravity sits with the oldest of the three, which is the opposite of how these households are usually weighted.

In a Silesian town where the industry has gone, the man with steady work is the one collecting debts from people who have none. Feliks Falk gives Lucjan Bohme 93 minutes and no cushion: an occupation that runs on other people's worst days, performed well, by someone who has filed mercy under another department. Most of the interest is in how completely the job accounts for him, and in the pressure the film accumulates while he is being efficient. Poland sent it to the Academy Awards. Unemployment is the town's condition and his opportunity, which is a nastier arrangement than a villain would be, since nobody involved is doing anything he is not entitled to do. The hardness belongs to the place. He only administers it.

Housing is the least cinematic emergency there is, and Joanna Kos-Krauze builds 105 minutes on it. A married couple, two children, and a housing problem that will not resolve: the ordering matters, because everything else bends around that first fact. Infidelity arrives, and exhaustion, and they behave less like causes than like weather produced by the pressure of living in rooms that belong to someone else. Nothing is enlarged for effect, which is exactly why it is hard to sit through. The Golden Lions at Gdynia went to it, and the Polish Film Award for best film as well. Domestic collapse rarely provides a moment that can be pointed to afterwards; it provides a long sequence of ordinary evenings in which two people run out of ways to be generous with each other.

Eighty-six minutes, a teenage girl, and a set of conditions she did not choose. Robert Gliński made Cześć, Tereska in 2001; it won at Gdynia and again at the Polish Film Awards, which is not the ordinary reception for a small picture about a poor family. The short runtime works as a discipline. There is no space for a survey of anything, so all of it has to arrive through one adolescent's day-to-day, with the adults present as circumstances rather than as people with plans of their own. What that buys is a particular kind of proximity: at that age a bad week and a bad life are not yet distinguishable from the inside, and a film this close has no way of assuring anyone they are different.

Tomasz is a physician and an atheist, and the diagnosis he is handed is one he can read without assistance. His ex-wife offers to pay for treatment in Paris; the lung cancer is already past the stage where an operation would use the money. Krzysztof Zanussi spends the remaining 97 minutes on what a trained sceptic does with a fixed quantity of time, which turns out to be experiments, conducted on his own days and on other people's, because testing things is the only method he was ever given. The film took a Golden George, and Poland sent it to the Academy Awards. A doctor's relation to his own body is professional before it is anything else, and that makes him the hardest subject a film about dying can take on: he cannot be told anything he does not already know.
